A2.text:
Leyla is fifteen, and she is a big fan of Samir Rza. Samir is the most famous singer in Azerbaijan. His rise to fame was very fast: two years ago nobody knew him, and now his songs are everywhere.

On Saturday, Samir came to a music shop in Baku to sign autographs. Leyla wanted to go, but her parents were at work. So her grandfather, Agasalim, went with her. He is seventy-four, and he does not like crowds.

They waited in the line for three hours. Outside, the paparazzi took photos of everyone. Leyla held her poster and talked about Samir all the time. “He is my role model,” she said. “He never has a scandal. Everybody loves him.”

At last it was Leyla's turn. Samir smiled and took her poster. Then he looked at her grandfather and stopped.

“Are you Agasalim Huseynov?” he asked. “My father played your songs every day. You are the reason I sing!”

Leyla did not understand. Her grandfather was a singer? He was a celebrity fifty years ago, but he never talked about it.

Samir gave Agasalim a pen and his own notebook. “Please,” he said. “Can I have your autograph?”

On the way home, Leyla asked a hundred questions. Her grandfather only laughed. “It was my fifteen minutes of fame,” he said. “Now eat your ice cream.”

options: He wants to be famous again
He doesn't think it is very important
questions.why: He only laughs, calls it his “fifteen minutes of fame” and talks about ice cream.

B1.text:
Leyla is fifteen, and her bedroom walls are covered with posters of Samir Rza. Like half the teenagers in Baku, she is a devoted fan. Samir's rise to fame was almost unbelievable: two years ago he was singing at weddings in Ganja, and now his songs play in every taxi and shopping centre.

When Samir announced that he would sign autographs at a music shop on Nizami Street, Leyla begged her parents to take her. They were both working, so the job went to her grandfather, Agasalim, a quiet man of seventy-four who usually avoids crowds and spends his afternoons reading the newspaper.

They stood in the queue for nearly three hours. Outside, a group of paparazzi photographed anyone who looked slightly interesting. Leyla talked non-stop. “Samir is my role model,” she explained. “He's kind, he works hard and he's never been in a single scandal. His reputation is perfect.” Agasalim just nodded and ate the sunflower seeds he had brought in his pocket.

Finally it was their turn. Samir signed Leyla's poster with a big smile — and then he noticed the old man behind her. His smile disappeared. He stood up.

“You're Agasalim Huseynov,” he said quietly. “My father had all your records. I learned to sing by copying your voice.”

Leyla stared at her grandfather. In the 1970s, it turned out, he had been a real celebrity, on television every week. Then one day he simply stopped. He was tired of living in the limelight, and he missed his privacy and his family.

Samir pushed a pen and his own notebook across the table. “Would you sign this for me?”

That evening the photo was all over the internet: the country's biggest star asking an old man for an autograph. Leyla printed it out and put it on her wall — right in the middle, above all the posters of Samir.

Samir recognises Leyla's grandfather as a famous singer

options: Living in a very bright house
Being the centre of public attention

options: She doesn't like Samir any more

questions.why: She keeps the Samir posters but puts the photo of her grandfather's moment “right in the middle”.

B2.text:
For two years, Leyla's life had revolved around Samir Rza. His rise to fame had been the kind of story magazines adore: a boy who sang at weddings in Ganja, a video recorded on a cheap phone and then, almost overnight, sold-out concerts at the Crystal Hall. Leyla, fifteen and fiercely loyal, considered herself his most devoted fan in Baku, and she had the posters to prove it.

So when Samir announced an autograph session at a music shop on Nizami Street, nothing was going to stop her. Her parents were working, which is how her grandfather Agasalim — seventy-four, allergic to crowds and deeply attached to his afternoon newspaper — found himself in a queue that stretched around the block.

They waited for nearly three hours while the paparazzi prowled the pavement, photographing anyone who might be worth a headline. Leyla filled the time with a lecture. Samir was her role model, she explained. Unlike other celebrities, he had never been involved in a single scandal; his reputation was spotless. Agasalim listened patiently, cracking sunflower seeds and saying very little.

When they finally reached the table, Samir signed Leyla's poster with his famous grin — and then caught sight of the old man behind her. The grin vanished. He rose slowly to his feet.

“Agasalim Huseynov,” he said, almost in a whisper. “My father wore out three copies of your record. I learned to sing by imitating you in the bathroom.”

Leyla turned to her grandfather as if she had never seen him before. It emerged, over the next few minutes, that in the 1970s he had spent years in the limelight, on television every Saturday night, until he walked away at the height of his career because he valued his privacy more than applause.

Samir slid a pen and his own battered notebook across the table. “Would you sign it? Please?”

By evening, the paparazzi's photo had gone everywhere: the nation's biggest star asking a pensioner for his autograph. Journalists called it a forgotten legacy. Agasalim called it nonsense. “I had my fifteen minutes of fame,” he said, folding his newspaper. “Then I had fifty years of dinners with your grandmother. Guess which I'd choose.”

Leyla didn't take the posters down. But the photo went up in the middle of the wall, bigger than all of them.

words.phrase: walked away at the height of his career
